rv.q: This staging by Elle While, the first for one of the German writer’s plays at the Globe, sits so securely in the wooden auditorium and communes so directly with the audience you feel the place could have been built for him.
She’s played by Globe chief Michelle Terry, whose superpower is her rare ability to slip into any part and seem born to play it – and this really is a winning turn.
As that other former Globe artistic director Mark Rylance did before her, Terry knows exactly how to play this wraparound space so as to draw in all spectators and her command is a delight to watch.
Thankfully, Terry is astonishingly good as Mother Courage.
The production does full justice in its portrait of complicated, imperfect and doggedly hopeful motherhood, too.
Flinging f-words in all directions and rounding off transactions with a defiant “ker-ching”, Terry’s Mother holds your attention, even if she tends to strike the same querulous tone throughout.
Rivers of emotion run through this work in ways that one does not typically associate with Brechtian performance.
Dark, distressing, funny and thoroughly entertaining, this production is a powerful and emotionally charged experience.
A topical translation of one of the great anti-war dramas proves another smart programming choice from Terry's Globe, and continues its rich vein of form.
So it was with Michelle Terry who ripped the throat out of Mother Courage at The Globe's press night on Friday evening.
The Globe’s outdoor space and tendency to incorporate music into the performance seem well-suited to this venue’s first production of a Brecht play.
Together these elements combine to make for a theatrical experiment that finds some novelty in creative risks, but not enough to make the production feel truly insightful or a knockout.
Michelle Terry has found a role that suits her ferocious charm and her combative energy, and she dominates the stage like a modern Boadicea.
It’s a bold, brave piece of programming that reaffirms Terry’s inspired leadership as an actor and artistic director.

For all its ambition and Terry’s remarkable energy in portraying a remarkably energetic woman, the vision of this production never resolves into a clear picture, too sharp at some times, too fuzzy at others.
It feels like a key work under Terry’s leadership.

This lively production directed by While (Pentabus Theatre’s artistic director) brings out Brecht’s innate theatricality as well as conveying his political message, in a show that is thoroughly entertaining and at times surprisingly moving.
